nameStory: Sweet peas earned their delightful name from their incredibly fragrant flowers that can perfume an entire garden on a warm summer evening. The 'sweet' refers to their intoxicating floral scent, while 'pea' comes from their membership in the pea family, with flowers that share the distinctive butterfly-like shape of garden peas.
description: Sweet pea is a climbing annual vine that reaches 3-6 feet tall when it has something to climb on. It produces delicate, butterfly-shaped flowers that come in purple in the wild form, though garden varieties bloom in many colors including pink, white, and red. The plant has distinctive compound leaves with two leaflets and curly tendrils that help it climb up fences, trellises, or other plants.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Butterfly-shaped blooms about 1-1.5 inches across with an incredibly sweet, perfume-like fragrance that you can smell from several feet away. Wild plants have purple flowers, but garden escapes may be pink, white, or other colors.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Compound leaves with exactly two oval leaflets and a curly tendril at the tip that feels springy to the touch and coils around supports like a tiny green corkscrew.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Climbing vine that scrambles up through other plants or structures, with weak, hollow stems that feel soft and somewhat brittle when gently squeezed.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Flattened pods about 2 inches long that rattle when shaken when mature, containing several round, hard peas inside.

habitat: Sweet peas are rarely found wild in New England, appearing mainly as garden escapes near homes, along roadsides, or in disturbed areas where seeds have been scattered. When they do establish, they prefer sunny spots with rich, well-drained soil and something to climb on like fences or shrubs.

seasonality.spring: Seeds germinate and young plants begin climbing, producing their first pairs of leaflets and tendrils.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming period with intensely fragrant flowers opening in the morning when their scent is strongest. Plants continue growing and climbing throughout the season.
seasonality.fall: Flowers fade and seed pods develop, turning brown and papery. Plants begin to die back as temperatures cool.
seasonality.winter: Dead stems may persist on supports, but the annual plants have died completely and won't return without new seeds.

funFact: Sweet peas are so powerfully fragrant that Victorian flower breeders actually tried to reduce their scent in some varieties because it was considered overwhelming for indoor bouquets - the opposite of what most flower breeding tries to achieve!
confusionNotes: Sweet pea is most easily confused with everlasting pea, but everlasting pea is a perennial that comes back each year, has broader leaflets, and typically lacks the intense fragrance. Remember: if it smells heavenly sweet, it's probably the annual sweet pea.
contextualKnowledge: Despite their name and pea-like appearance, sweet pea seeds are toxic to humans and should never be eaten, unlike garden peas. This beautiful climbing flower is grown purely for ornament and fragrance, not food.
compareHints: Among its Lathyrus relatives in New England, sweet pea stands out for its incredible fragrance and annual growth habit. Seaside pea grows on beaches and has thicker, more succulent leaves, while broad-leaved everlasting pea is perennial with wider leaflets and much less fragrant flowers. Sweet pea's combination of intense scent and delicate climbing habit makes it unique in the genus.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England's Lathyrus species, seaside pea is the only one with those distinctive thick, waxy blue-green leaves and strict beach habitat.
Among New England's sweet peas, broad-leaved sweet pea stands out with its distinctly wide leaflets - most others like meadow pea have narrow, grass-like leaflets.
Among New England's wild peas, narrow-leaved everlasting-pea stands out with its bold pink flowers and strongly winged stems.
Among New England's wild peas, meadow pea stands out with its bright yellow flowers - most of its relatives like seaside pea and marsh pea have purple or pink blooms.
Among its Lathyrus relatives, marsh pea is distinguished by its wetland habitat and pinkish-purple flowers.

Unlike the broad-leaved sweet pea which has wider leaflets and no tubers, or the seaside pea which has 6-12 leaflets, tuberous pea is distinguished by its simple two-leaflet arrangement and underground tuber system.
Unlike its Lathyrus relatives in New England, spring vetch lacks the climbing tendrils found on species like broad-leaved sweet pea and narrow-leaved everlasting-pea.

Among its Lathyrus relatives in New England, pale vetchling stands out for its uniquely subdued flower color – while seaside pea has purple flowers, meadow pea is bright yellow, and broad-leaved sweet pea shows off in magenta.
Grass pea stands out from its New England Lathyrus cousins primarily by its unique brick-red flowers - no other sweet pea or vetchling in our region shares this color.
